name: New Year
description: Endings, beginnings, and the resolve that comes with a turned page.
author: Quips Editorial

quotes.content:
Ring out, wild bells, to the wild sky,
The flying cloud, the frosty light:
The year is dying in the night;
Ring out, wild bells, and let him die.
quotes.source: In Memoriam A.H.H., Canto CVI, stanza 1 (1850)
quotes.notes: The opening of the canto that gave the English-speaking world its midnight bell-ringing liturgy.

quotes.content:
Ring out the old, ring in the new,
Ring, happy bells, across the snow:
The year is going, let him go;
Ring out the false, ring in the true.
quotes.source: In Memoriam A.H.H., Canto CVI, stanza 2 (1850)
quotes.notes: The stanza that supplied the phrase every New Year editorial has used since.

quotes.content:
Ring in the valiant man and free,
The larger heart, the kindlier hand;
Ring out the darkness of the land,
Ring in the Christ that is to be.
quotes.source: In Memoriam A.H.H., Canto CVI, stanza 8 (1850)
quotes.notes: The stanza that closes the sequence, still ringing out the darkness of the land even as it turns toward what should be rung in.

quotes.content:
Should auld acquaintance be forgot,
And never brought to mind?
Should auld acquaintance be forgot,
And days o' lang syne?
quotes.source: "Auld Lang Syne," The Scots Musical Museum, vol. 5 (1796)
quotes.notes: Burns sent the song to James Johnson as an old fragment he had taken down from an old man's singing, then finished himself — a claim he made to George Thomson. The familiar fourth line, "And auld lang syne", is in neither primary printing.

quotes.content:
And for auld lang syne, my jo,
For auld lang syne,
We'll tak a cup o' kindness yet,
For auld lang syne.
quotes.source: "Auld Lang Syne," chorus, The Scots Musical Museum, vol. 5 (1796)
quotes.notes: The chorus sung at midnight across the world, usually with the words half-remembered; "auld lang syne" means old long since, or times gone by. The Museum's text opens "And for"; Thomson's 1799 printing reads "my dear" for "my jo".

quotes.content: No one ever regarded the First of January with indifference.
quotes.source: "New Year's Eve," Essays of Elia (1823); first published in The London Magazine (January 1821)
quotes.notes: Lamb's premise: everyone has two birthdays, and this is the one the whole world keeps at once.

quotes.content: Of all sounds of all bells — (bells, the music nighest bordering upon heaven) — most solemn and touching is the peal which rings out the Old Year.
quotes.source: "New Year's Eve," Essays of Elia (1823); first published in The London Magazine (January 1821)
quotes.notes: Written nearly thirty years before Tennyson's wild bells, and probably in their ancestry.

quotes.content:
The land's sharp features seemed to be
The Century's corpse outleant,
His crypt the cloudy canopy,
The wind his death-lament.
quotes.source: "The Darkling Thrush," The Graphic (29 December 1900), printed as "By the Century's Deathbed"
quotes.notes: Hardy's poem of the century's end; the 1901 first edition datelines it only "December 1900", though the manuscript carries a deleted 1899.

quotes.content:
That I could think there trembled through
His happy good-night air
Some blessed Hope, whereof he knew
And I was unaware.
quotes.source: "The Darkling Thrush," The Graphic (29 December 1900)
quotes.notes: The last four lines: hope granted to the bird and withheld from the poet, which is as far toward optimism as Hardy goes.

quotes.content: Remember ye not the former things, neither consider the things of old. Behold, I will do a new thing; now it shall spring forth; shall ye not know it?
quotes.source: Isaiah 43:18–19, King James Version (1611)
quotes.notes: Spoken to exiles in Babylon, which is why it reads as a promise rather than a suggestion.

quotes.content: Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.
quotes.source: 2 Corinthians 5:17, King James Version (1611)
quotes.notes: The verse most often read at watchnight services on the last night of the year.

quotes.content: It is of the LORD's mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness.
quotes.source: Lamentations 3:22–23, King James Version (1611)
quotes.notes: A claim about renewal made in the middle of a book of grief over a destroyed city.

quotes.content: So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom.
quotes.source: Psalm 90:12, King James Version (1611)
quotes.notes: From the psalm ascribed to Moses, and the oldest form of the argument that counting time is what makes it worth anything.

quotes.content: Brethren, I count not myself to have apprehended: but this one thing I do, forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth unto those things which are before.
quotes.source: Philippians 3:13, King James Version (1611)
quotes.notes: Written from prison, and the reason the phrase about forgetting what is behind turns up on so many January pulpits.

quotes.content: Nothing, Lucilius, is ours, except time.
quotes.source: Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter I, trans. Richard M. Gummere, Loeb Classical Library (1917)
quotes.notes: Seneca to Lucilius at Letter I, section 3, on time as the one possession worth hoarding. Gummere's Loeb translation (1917).

quotes.content: It is not that we have a short space of time, but that we waste much of it.
quotes.source: On the Shortness of Life, I, trans. John W. Basore, Loeb Classical Library (1932)
quotes.notes: Seneca's whole essay is an argument against the complaint that life is too short; wording is Basore's, as other translators render it very differently.

quotes.content: Do not act as if thou wert going to live ten thousand years. Death hangs over thee. While thou livest, while it is in thy power, be good.
quotes.source: Meditations, Book IV, 17, trans. George Long (1862)
quotes.notes: Long's Victorian English is the version most readers know; modern translations drop the thees and lose the weight.

quotes.content: Dum loquimur, fugerit invida aetas: carpe diem, quam minimum credula postero.
quotes.source: Odes, Book I, xi, lines 7–8 (c. 23 BCE)
quotes.notes: Given in Horace's Latin because every English rendering differs: while we speak, envious time flies; seize the day, trusting the next as little as you can.

quotes.content:
For last year's words belong to last year's language
And next year's words await another voice.
quotes.source: "Little Gidding," II (1942); Four Quartets (1943)
quotes.notes: Spoken in the encounter with the familiar compound ghost, during a wartime dawn after an air raid.

quotes.content:
What we call the beginning is often the end
And to make an end is to make a beginning.
The end is where we start from.
quotes.source: "Little Gidding," V (1942); Four Quartets (1943)
quotes.notes: The opening of the last section of the last quartet, which is itself an ending arguing with the idea of endings.

quotes.content: I hope that in this year to come, you make mistakes. Because if you are making mistakes, then you are making new things, trying new things, learning, living, pushing yourself, changing yourself, changing your world. You're doing things you've never done before, and more importantly, you're Doing Something.
quotes.source: "My New Year Wish," journal.neilgaiman.com (31 December 2011)
quotes.notes: Posted to his own journal on New Year's Eve and reposted by him most years since.

quotes.content: May your coming year be filled with magic and dreams and good madness. I hope you read some fine books and kiss someone who thinks you're wonderful, and don't forget to make some art — write or draw or build or sing or live as only you can. And I hope, somewhere in the next year, you surprise yourself.
quotes.source: journal.neilgaiman.com, untitled New Year's Eve entry (31 December 2001)
quotes.notes: Source axis fails: the 2001 entry names the year — "May your 2002 be filled with magic and dreams and good madness" — and contains a transposition Gaiman later fixed. This is the generalized wording he reposts, which no single dated post has been matched to. The title "A New Year Wish" is not his.

quotes.content:
One day you finally knew
what you had to do, and began,
though the voices around you
kept shouting
their bad advice—
quotes.source: "The Journey," Dream Work (1986)
quotes.notes: The beginning of a poem about leaving, in which the decisive act happens in the first line and the rest is consequence.

quotes.content: How we spend our days is, of course, how we spend our lives.
quotes.source: The Writing Life (1989), ch. 2
quotes.notes: Dillard on schedules, page 32, in the chapter about how a working day is spent; the sentence continues "What we do with this hour, and that one, is what we are doing."

quotes.content: I think we are well advised to keep on nodding terms with the people we used to be, whether we find them attractive company or not.
quotes.source: "On Keeping a Notebook," Slouching Towards Bethlehem (1968)
quotes.notes: The argument for looking back at the year rather than over it.

quotes.content: Dost thou love Life? then do not squander Time; for that's the Stuff Life is made of.
quotes.source: Poor Richard's Almanack (1746); repeated in "The Way to Wealth" (1758)
quotes.notes: From the June calendar page of Poor Richard's Almanack for 1746. Franklin reworked it for The Way to Wealth in 1758 — "But dost thou love Life, then do not squander Time" — softening the question mark and semicolon to commas.

quotes.content: The object of a New Year is not that we should have a new year. It is that we should have a new soul and a new nose; new feet, a new backbone, new ears, and new eyes.
quotes.source: "January One," Daily News, London (1904); collected in Lunacy and Letters (1958)
quotes.notes: Chesterton on resolutions as renovation rather than bookkeeping. Long reprinted from A Chesterton Calendar without its origin; the essay behind it is "January One".

quotes.content: New Year's Day: Now is the accepted time to make your regular annual good resolutions. Next week you can begin paving hell with them as usual.
quotes.source: "New Year's Day," Virginia City Territorial Enterprise (probably 1 January 1863); Mark Twain Project, Early Tales & Sketches, vol. 1, no. 35
quotes.notes: Clemens writing as the Enterprise's own local reporter, not a correspondent. It survives as a single clipping in his scrapbook, which the Mark Twain Project uses as copy-text.

quotes.content: Write it on your heart that every day is the best day in the year.
quotes.source: "Works and Days," Society and Solitude (1870)
quotes.notes: Rejected by an earlier pass as unlocatable; it is verbatim Emerson, a few lines after "the present hour is not the critical, decisive hour".

quotes.content: We are what we repeatedly do. Excellence, then, is not an act but a habit.
quotes.source: The Story of Philosophy, ch. II (1926)
quotes.notes: Durant's own summary of Aristotle, to whom it is almost always misattributed. He writes it mid-sentence with a lowercase "we" and no comma after "act".
